ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude? My Experience Working with Code
Why benchmark scores don't always matter in real projects, and how different AI models handle actual bug fixing.

Lately, I’ve been thinking more and more about how much AI has changed the way developers work.

Not that long ago, we were used to finding bugs ourselves, reading documentation, checking Stack Overflow, staring at the same piece of code for hours and thinking, *“Where on earth is the problem?..”*

Now you can just show the code to an AI and ask:
> “What’s wrong here?”

But there’s an interesting thing I’ve noticed. All these AIs look incredibly smart... until you give them a real problem from a real project.

I decided to compare three tools that seem to be everywhere these days: **ChatGPT**, **Gemini**, and **Claude**. 

I didn’t run any serious scientific tests. This isn’t a benchmark or a proper research study. It’s simply my own experience from working with code. And that’s exactly why I wanted to share it. Because sometimes the numbers and rankings say one thing, but when you’re actually sitting in front of a bug in your project, things can feel completely different.

---

### ChatGPT
I like ChatGPT, and I use it for all sorts of things. It’s good at explaining concepts, helping with ideas, and discussing architecture.

But during one coding task, I had a rather interesting experience:
* I showed it the problem and asked it to find the bug.
* I expected the AI to look at the code, understand where the actual problem was, and suggest a fix.
* Instead, it started looking in completely different places.
* Then it suggested changes in other files, and then a few more changes...

And at some point I thought: *“Hang on. Are we even fixing the right problem here?”* I had to bring it back to the original issue several times.

---

### Gemini
I had a pretty similar experience with Gemini.

It also suggested different approaches, changed things, and explained some of its ideas, but I didn’t get that feeling that the AI actually understood where the problem was. It felt more like it was changing things *around* the problem rather than finding the actual cause.

---

### Claude
And then I tried Claude. That’s when something really surprised me.

I gave it the exact same problem, and it found the place I had been looking for almost immediately. No long detour through the project. No attempt to rewrite half the files. No:

> “Well, we could also change this component... and this file... and maybe try a completely different approach...”

It simply pointed to the problem and explained why it was happening. I made the change. **And it worked.**

---

### Quality Over Quantity

That’s why I think moments like this show the difference between AI tools much better than impressive presentations ever can.

When you’re working on a real project, you don’t always need an AI that can write 500 lines of code in a minute. Sometimes you just need an AI that looks at those 500 lines and says:

> **“Here’s the problem.”**

Right now, out of these three tools, I personally prefer Claude for coding. What I especially like is how it handles existing code. Creating something new is one thing, but finding a bug in a project that already exists, understanding how different files are connected, making sure you don’t break something that already works, and changing only what actually needs to be changed... that’s a completely different story.

---

### The Evolution of AI Development

Of course, I’m only talking about what I’ve actually been able to test myself. I don’t want to say: *“Claude is the best AI on the market.”* That’s a pretty big statement.

Today there’s one model, tomorrow there’s another. A model that everyone was calling revolutionary yesterday can be overtaken by a new version a few months later. Things are moving incredibly fast:
* **Google** keeps releasing new Gemini models with a strong focus on coding and agentic workflows.
* **OpenAI** is developing Codex as a dedicated tool for real software development and working with repositories.
* **Anthropic** is pushing Claude heavily towards programming, putting a lot of focus on coding capabilities and newer iterations.

So I think the question we should be asking now isn’t really: *“Which AI is the smartest?”* 

Maybe the better question is: **“Which AI works best for what I actually need?”**

---

### Working Alongside AI

We’re slowly moving from a situation where AI simply writes code to one where AI actually works alongside us on a project. And honestly, I find that much more interesting.

Being a good developer isn’t about being the person who can write the most lines of code. Sometimes being a good developer means:
* Knowing how to ask the right question.
* Giving the AI the right context.
* Explaining what already works.
* Telling it what must not be changed.
* Asking it to find the cause first, and only then suggest a solution.

AI is getting better and better, but the more powerful these models become, the more important it is to understand what exactly we want from them. 

For now, I’m simply watching how all of this develops and trying different tools. Based on what I’ve actually tested myself, Claude is my choice for coding at the moment. Not because someone told me it’s number one, but because when I genuinely needed help, it found the bug.

How Pivoting to Micro-SaaS Turned 6 Months of Failure into Growth
A candid story about failing for six months with a generic SaaS product, discovering a mindset shift via YouTube, and pivoting to customer-led growth.

Photo by artmozai on Pinterest
For six grueling months, my morning routine was always the same: open my analytics dashboard, stare at the flatline, and feel a slow burn of exhaustion. I had poured all my savings and hundreds of sleepless hours of coding into this project. The result? Exactly three paying clients—two of whom were my close friends out of pity. I had built yet another SaaS task management tool, basically trying to clone Trello and Notion. I was genuinely furious and confused as to why freelancers and agencies weren’t running to me with their credit cards. I felt powerless, bitter, and completely burned out. --- ## The Wake-Up Call One night, while aimlessly scrolling YouTube to kill time, the algorithm pushed a video by a bootstrapped IT founder into my feed. I clicked out of pure boredom, fully expecting another "guru" selling fake dreams. Instead, every word he spoke felt like a personal attack. He called out the exact mistakes I was making. I sat there in the dark, cold sweat breaking out, realizing I had built my entire startup on a completely broken foundation: * **No real research:** I had locked myself in a room, building features *I* thought were cool, without talking to a single target user. * **No competitive clarity:** I was trying to fight industry giants head-on with zero differentiation. * **Pure money focus:** I was obsessed with recurring revenue (MRR) and subscription tiers, completely ignoring actual human value. * **Zero personal conviction:** I asked myself the hardest question—*Would I actually pay for and use my own product every day?* The honest answer was **no**. It was bloated, generic, and solved nothing specific. That night, my mindset completely shifted. I had nothing left to lose, so I decided to throw away my ego and follow the framework. --- ## The Pivot: Research Over Assumptions I stripped the product down and went straight to **customer development**. I reached out to dozens of digital agencies and creative studios, requesting short 15-minute calls just to listen to their workflows. I quickly discovered a massive, shared pain point: nobody needed another task board. What was actually killing their productivity was the chaos of **getting media assets and documents approved by clients**. Stakeholders lost links, feedback was scattered across email threads, and deadlines constantly slipped. I shifted my focus from *"How do I sell a subscription?"* to **"How can I eliminate this approval headache?"** I rebuilt the tool into a hyper-focused micro-SaaS: a lightweight platform where agencies could send media files to clients for one-click approvals, no client registration required. It was so fast and seamless that I instantly started using it for my own projects. --- ## The Growth Strategy: Partnerships & Guerrilla Marketing Once I had a product people actually wanted, I avoided competing with giants like Google Drive or Frame.io. Instead, I pursued **strategic partnerships**. I reached out to a popular agency CRM platform and built a native integration. We pooled our strengths: their users got a seamless asset-approval workflow, and my tool got instant exposure to their established user base. That single integration generated a massive surge in active users within weeks. To launch publicly without a massive ad budget, we skipped boring search ads and went for a **creative, non-standard approach**: 1. We built an interactive **"Client Revision Cost Calculator"** where agencies could estimate how many billable hours they lost to email back-and-forth. 2. We launched an honest, relatable thread on X (Twitter) showcasing the most absurd client feedback stories submitted by the community. The content went viral. Product communities, Telegram channels, and agency hubs picked it up organically. --- ## The Takeaway The clients and sustainable revenue didn't show up when I was obsessing over their wallets. They arrived the moment I stopped trying to make a quick buck and started genuinely solving a real, painful problem. *** **What about you? If you're building or planning a product right now, what's the single biggest pain point your target users are facing—and have you validated it with them yet?**

The Pivot: Research Over Assumptions

I quickly discovered a massive, shared pain point: nobody needed another task board. What was actually killing their productivity was the chaos of getting media assets and documents approved by clients. Stakeholders lost links, feedback was scattered across email threads, and deadlines constantly slipped.

I shifted my focus from “How do I sell a subscription?” to “How can I eliminate this approval headache?”

I rebuilt the tool into a hyper-focused micro-SaaS: a lightweight platform where agencies could send media files to clients for one-click approvals, no client registration required. It was so fast and seamless that I instantly started using it for my own projects.

The Growth Strategy: Partnerships & Guerrilla Marketing

Once I had a product people actually wanted, I avoided competing with giants like Google Drive or Frame.io. Instead, I pursued strategic partnerships.

I reached out to a popular agency CRM platform and built a native integration. We pooled our strengths: their users got a seamless asset-approval workflow, and my tool got instant exposure to their established user base. That single integration generated a massive surge in active users within weeks.

To launch publicly without a massive ad budget, we skipped boring search ads and went for a creative, non-standard approach:

  1. We built an interactive “Client Revision Cost Calculator” where agencies could estimate how many billable hours they lost to email back-and-forth.
  2. We launched an honest, relatable thread on X (Twitter) showcasing the most absurd client feedback stories submitted by the community.

The content went viral. Product communities, Telegram channels, and agency hubs picked it up organically.

The Takeaway

The clients and sustainable revenue didn’t show up when I was obsessing over their wallets. They arrived the moment I stopped trying to make a quick buck and started genuinely solving a real, painful problem.

Why Senior Software Engineers Burn Out
Why senior software engineers burn out by trying to handle everything alone, and how asking for help and delegating work can make a difference.

Recently, I was watching one of my colleagues, a senior software engineer, and noticed something interesting.

After he was promoted from Middle to Senior Engineer, he started working even more. I think he wanted to show that he was really ready for the new position and could handle any task.

At first, I didn't think much about it. But over time, I started to notice something that is common with senior software engineers: burnout can come from trying to solve everything alone.

He almost never asked for help. When a difficult task came up, he tried to solve it himself. If something needed to be designed from scratch, he also took care of it. Even when other people on the team could help, he preferred to try everything by himself first.

At first, it actually looked good. He was very responsible, worked hard, and always tried to do everything well.

But after a few months, I started to notice some changes.

He looked tired. Sometimes it was easy to see that he was very worried about work. Before, he often talked about his tasks with real interest. Later, work became more like a source of stress for him.

The most interesting thing was that everything looked fine from the outside. He continued working, finished his tasks, and did his job. But it was clear that it was becoming harder for him to keep the same energy.

One day, his manager asked him:
> “Why don't you communicate more with the team? Why don't you ask for help?”

I think this question surprised him.

He was used to thinking that as a Senior Engineer, he should find solutions himself and handle difficult tasks on his own. Maybe he even thought that asking for help would make him look weak.

After that conversation, he started to change his approach a little.

He began discussing tasks with his colleagues more often. If he didn't know the best way to do something, he could simply ask someone for their opinion. Sometimes he delegated part of the work instead of doing everything himself.

And slowly, it became clear that work was getting easier for him.

It turned out that everyone on the team had their own experience. One colleague could quickly find a technical solution, another could notice a problem that nobody had seen before, and a third could suggest a simpler way to do the same thing.

Sometimes, all you need is a ten-minute conversation with someone to understand something that you could have been thinking about for hours.

I often think about this story because the desire to do everything yourself doesn't happen only at work.

Sometimes a person simply wants to be strong. They don't want to bother anyone, they don't want to show that something is difficult, so they continue to carry everything alone.

From the outside, such a person may look very confident and independent.

But inside, the story can be completely different.

* They are tired, but they keep working.
* Things are difficult, but they say everything is fine.
* They don't know what to do next, but they still try to find the answer alone.

And probably the hardest thing is to notice this moment in time.

Because sometimes a person doesn't need another piece of advice or another task.

Sometimes they just need someone nearby to ask:
**“Can I help you?”**
